en: Now begins the *Prātiśākhyapradīpa-śikṣā*.
I bow to Heramba, the remover of obstacles, and to Sarasvatī; by the mere act of bowing to these two, the multitude of obstacles is destroyed. (1)
Having carefully and thoroughly examined the Prātiśākhyas and the Śikṣās,
this work was composed by the wise Bālakṛṣṇa, son of Sadāśiva, for the easy understanding of Vedic students and for the perfect accomplishment of their recitation.
The *Śikṣā* known as the *Prātiśākhyapradīpa* is now correctly examined.
Now follows the method of Vedic study. Regarding this, Yājñavalkya says:
"One should first employ the *praṇava*, and immediately after that, the *vyāhṛtis*."
Then, having recited the Sāvitrī in the proper sequence, he should begin the Vedas.
Keeping his hands joined and placed above his knees,
and having obtained the permission of his teacher, he should recite without his mind being directed elsewhere.
Then, having placed the right hand on the third part of the thighs,
with a serene mind and the face slightly bent downward,
one should withdraw the hands, eyes, and mind firmly like a tortoise withdrawing its limbs.
Established in himself, tranquil, and fearless, the wise man should pronounce the phonemes.
He should not bend them, nor suppress them, nor over-articulate them, nor sing them, nor cause them to tremble;
just as he pronounced the phonemes at the beginning, so should he conclude them.
Fixing one's gaze on the tip of the hand, one should reflect upon the meaning of the Vedas;
one should correctly pronounce the phonemes with both the hand and the mouth,
for both the tone and the hand exist simultaneously.

One who has dropped [the syllables] from the hand or dropped them from the correct accent does not enjoy the fruit of the Veda. One who is deformed, one with a hanging lip, one who is indistinct, one who is nasal, one who stammers,
or one whose tongue is bound, is not capable of pronouncing the phonemes correctly.
The *culurnnaukā*, the *sphuṭa*, the *daṇḍī*, the *svastika*, the form of the *muṣṭikā*, and the *paraśu* as the seventh—these indeed are the defects of the hand.
Now, regarding the sequence for moving the hands, it is stated in that same source: "That which occurs upon the upper joint of the thumb, above the index finger..."
One should move the hand only as far as the region of the *prādeśa*.
The *udātta* accent is produced by a downward movement at the forehead; the *pracaya* is at the tip of the nose;
the *anudātta* is at the region of the heart; while the *svarita*, *jātya*, and other accents are formed transversely.
One should know that in the case of a *svarita* [accent], it is two finger-breadths; in the case of a *nipāta*, six finger-breadths;
and in the case of an *utthāna*, nine finger-breadths—this is the definition of the *svarita*.
And so it is stated in the *Pratijñāsūtra*:
The *anudātta* (unaccented) is at the heart, the *udātta* (acute) is at the top of the head, and the *svarita* (circumflex) is at the root of the ear.

Now follows the investigation of accents (*svaravicāra*). Thus it has been said: "There is the high accent (*ucca-svara*), the low accent (*nīca-svara*), and the circumflex accent (*svarita-svara*) itself; the threefold system of accents (*traisvaryam*) is dominated by these vowels, and by means of them, the consonant also possesses an accent."
Now, the definitions of the acute (*udātta*), grave (*anudātta*), and circumflex (*svarita*) accents are stated;

likewise in the *Prātiśākhya*: 1. "The high-pitched is acute": A vowel produced in the upper part [of the vocal tract] shall be designated as acute (*udātta*). For example: *agnāi*. And so forth, such as "the low-pitched is grave" (*udāttādanudāttaḥ*). Passages concerning the acute accent: 2. "The low-pitched is grave": A vowel produced in the lower part [of the vocal tract] shall be grave (*anudātta*). For example: *ārṣeya* (from *ṛṣīṇām*). Passages concerning the grave accent: 3. "After an acute, a grave becomes circumflex" (*udāttāccānudāttaṃ svaritam*). Passages concerning the circumflex accent:

An unaccented (anudātta) syllable following an accented (udātta) syllable becomes circumflex (svarita), provided it is separated from the preceding accent by a consonant. For example: *svāhā hisma* [hi ṣmma]. An unaccented syllable following an accented or circumflex syllable becomes circumflex when followed by an accented syllable or a circumflex syllable. When followed by an accented syllable (*udāttapara*), as in: *svāhā somāya*, *svargyāya* [svaḥ gyāya], *prasave’śśvinoḥ*, *parameṣṭṭhyabhidhītaḥ*, *sucīveti*. When followed by a circumflex syllable (*svaritapara*), as in: *svāhā svarṇārkkaḥ*, and so forth. A circumflex vowel is said to possess both [an acute and a grave] quality.

A vowel produced in both the upward and downward portions [of the articulation] shall be designated as *svarita*. For example: *svaḥ* (in *svo rāyaḥ*) and *dhānyam asi*. Now, eight internal subdivisions of the *svarita* itself are described as "tones" (*svara*). And so says Yājñavalkya: "I shall declare the eight tones and their very definitions: the *jātya*, the *abhinihita*, the *kṣaipra*, and another, the *praśliṣṭa*; the one known as *tairovyañjana*, likewise the *tairovirāmaka*; the *pādavṛtta*, and similarly the *tāthābhāvya*—these are the tones. (13–14)

Thus it is said. In that regard, the individual characteristics are stated. And so it is in the *Prātiśākhya*: "In a single word, one preceded by a low [pitch] and accompanied by a *yava* is the *jātya*. In a single word, a vowel preceded by a low pitch—that is, preceded by an *anudātta* (unaccented) syllable—or joined with the letter *y*, is to be understood as the *jātya* accent. The phrase "preceded by a low pitch" is a qualifying attribute according to its possibility; there are also cases where it is not preceded by such. An example of being preceded by a low pitch is: *dhānyam asi*; an example of not being preceded by such is: *kanyā iva*; and an example of not being preceded by such is: *svaddeveṣu*. And likewise says Yājñavalkya:

In a single word, a vowel preceded by a low-pitched (nīca) vowel is desired to be of the *jāti* type, even if it is not preceded [by another vowel], provided it is followed by one; this applies to *dhānya*, *kanyā*, and *svar* as well. 15. Seven accents beginning with the acute (*udātta*) are to be understood when they follow [others]: the *abhinihita*, *kṣaipra*, *praśliṣṭa*, *tairovyañjana*, *tairovirāma*, *pādavṛtta*, and *tāthābhāvya*. Eight [accents] follow a low-pitched vowel. 8.

The *abhinihita*, *kṣaipra*, and *praśliṣṭa* [sandhis] occur when followed by a low-pitched vowel (*nīcasvara*). When an *a*-vowel is elided after the acute (*udātta*) vowels *e* or *o*, that [resulting] accent is called *abhinihita*. For example: *te 'psarasām*, *te 'vantum*, *vedo 'si*, *stupo 'si*. And likewise Yājñavalkya says: "When an *a*-vowel and a *riphita* [consonant] are elided after the acute vowels *e* and *o*, they know that [resulting] accent to be *abhinihita*. An exception to this is stated: it does not occur in the word *deśe*.

In the word *deśa*, this vowel *e* does not become an *abhinidhāna-svarita* even when the *ā* of the word *abhavat* has been elided, as in *deśe'bhavat*. Regarding the rule *yu-varṇaiḥ*: "When the vowels *i* and *u* (*yu*), being acute (*udātta*) and followed by an unaccented (*anudātta*) vowel, are joined respectively with the consonants *y* and *v* (*yakāra-vakārau*), then the *kṣaipra* accent occurs. For example: *tri-ambakam* → *tryambakam*; *vvājī-arvvan* → *vājyarvvan*; *nu-indra* → *nvindra*; *dru-annaḥ* → *drvannaḥ*. And so says Yājñavalkya:

When the vowels *i* and *u*, along with their corresponding semivowels *y* and *v*, are always subjectively acute (*udātta*) when followed by an anudātta vowel, one should know this as the characteristic of the *kṣaipra* sandhi. (17) An *i*-vowel that is short on both sides is called *praśliṣṭa*. (12)

When a short *ikāra* is acute (*udātta*) and the following short *ikāra* is grave (*anudātta*), when these two are joined together, there arises the *praśliṣṭa* accent. For example: *abhi indhatām* becomes *abhīndhatām*; *srucīva*. And so says Yājñavalkya: "Where an *ikāra* is seen joined with another *ikāra*, and the acute is joined with the grave, that is the *praśliṣṭa* accent. (18) An accent joined with a consonant is called *tairovyañjana*. (13)

A vowel followed by a consonant that precedes an acute accent (udātta) is designated as *tairovyañjana*. For example: *iḍe*, *rante*. And likewise Yājñavalkya says: "Whatever [vowel] is preceded by an acute accent and joined with a consonant—this, containing many vowels, is designated as *tairovyañjana*. (19) A pause occurring within a word-division (*udavagraha*) is called *tairovirāma*. (14)

That which has an acute (udātta) *avagraha* is designated as *tairovirāma*. This occurs in all compound words (*samastapada*), because of the mention of *avagraha*. However, in the absence of an *avagraha*, it is simply *tairovyañjana*. For example: *gopatāv iti go-patau*; *yajñapatimiti yajña-patim*. And so says Yājñavalkya: "One should know that [svarita] which follows immediately after an *avagraha* is *tairovirāma*, provided that the *avagraha* is acute. [This concludes the section on] the characteristic of *vivṛtti*, namely *pādavṛtta*. 15. 20.

The interval between two vowels is called *vivṛtti*. That which is characterized by this [interval] is termed *pādavṛtta*; the meaning is that it is separated by a *vivṛtti*. For example: *dhruvā asadan* / *dhruvā'asadan*, *kā īm* / *kā'īm*. And likewise Yājñavalkya says: "If a *vivṛtti* is observed between a vowel (*svara*) and a circumflexed vowel (*svarita*), it becomes a *svāra-pādavṛtta*; 'śvitra āditya' is the illustration. Wherever a *vivṛtti* is observed during the interval of time between two vowels, [it is so designated].

That *svāra* [svarita] which occurs at the end of a word-division (*pādavṛtta*) is illustrated by the example *akā'īm*. (22) A *tāthābhāvya* is a *svara* that begins with an acute accent (*udātta*) and ends with an acute accent, while having a grave accent (*nīca*) at the word-division (*avagraha*). For example, in *tanūnapptra*, it is *tanū* | *napptre*; [it is pronounced as] *tanūnapāt* [with the division] *tanū* | *napāt*. And likewise Yājñavalkya says: "Between two acute syllables, there shall be a grave word-division; this is the *tāthābhāvya*, characterized by a tremor (*kampa*). *Tanūnapptra* is the illustration. (23)

According to the opinion of some, there is no eighth [type of] *tāthābhāvya*, because the *tāthābhāvya* consisting of a pause (*kampa*) has been rejected in the *Saṃhitā-pāṭha* of the Vājasaneyins. And it is stated in the Mādhyandina-Śikṣā: "When, according to the Aujjihāyanakas who follow the Mādhyandina school, there is an avagraha between a low and a high tone at any point, there occurs the *tāthābhāvya* pause;
'tanūnaptre' is the illustration. In the *Pada-pāṭha*, there indeed exists the accent called 'pause' (*kampa*). (24–25)
Thus, the eight vowels have been explained along with their illustrations. Regarding the acute accent (*udātta*): "Having struck straight down, one strikes further down. (17)

Having struck down the *svarita* accent so that it becomes straight (*ṛju*) and like an *anudātta*, it is then struck down even further and made low (*nīcī*) when followed by an *udātta* accent—this applies to the *jāti*, *abhinihita*, *kṣaipra*, and *praśliṣṭa* types. For example: *svaḥ* (as in) *dyauriva*; *svardyauriva*; *prasave aśśvinoḥ*; *ni atriṇam*; *sruci iva*. Why does it say "when followed by an *udātta*"? [Because in cases like] *dhānnyam asiṃ* or *vaiṣṇavyau*, it is not so. Now he states the definition of the *pracaya* accent: "That which follows a *svarita* and is *anudātta* consists of one or more syllables. (18)

An unaccented (*anudātta*) syllable following a circumflex (*svarita*)—whether it be one or several syllables—should be pronounced with the same pitch as an acute (*udātta*). This very accent is designated by Vedic scholars as *pracaya*, *pracita*, *praco*, *nicita*, or "composed of acute" (*udāttamaya*). It should be demonstrated by holding the hand level with the tip of the nose, according to the statement in the *Yājñavalkya-śikṣā*: "The *pracaya* is at the tip of the nose. [Examples: *yajñapatiḥ*; *adya'rṣa'ārṣeyaḥ*. [Rule 20: There is no circumflex (*svarita*) that arises immediately after an acute (*udātta*).

An unaccented vowel following a *svarita* does not undergo *pracaya* (the accentual rise) when followed by an acute (*udātta*) or a *svarita*. For example: *dṛḍhaṃ*, *hasva mā*, *tanacmi viṣṇo*, *sādannyaṃ vidathyam*. An unaccented vowel following an acute becomes acute; one following a *svarita* becomes *svarita*. Where both rules apply simultaneously, there is a conflict (*vipratiṣedha*), and the subsequent rule prevails, as in *sūnave agne* and *adyūtye avase*. This concludes the section on the rules for accents. Now, the euphonic combination of accents (*svarasaṃdhi*) is described. "In the *Ṛk-prātiśākhya*"—this is the governing heading (*adhikāra*). "The euphonic combination of the end of a word and the beginning of a word."

Whatever *sandhi*-operation is prescribed here shall apply between the end of a word and the beginning of a word. By the rule "When a vowel follows, a non-palatal [semivowel] becomes a future [element], provided there is a semivowel (*antasthā*) to follow," the designation "future" (*bhāvī*) is stated. Those vowels—*i*, *u*, *ṛ*, and *lṛ*—bearing the designation "future," when followed by a vowel, undergo a transformation into the corresponding semivowels (*antasthā*) *y*, *v*, *r*, and *l* respectively. For example: *punāmy acchidreṇa* [becomes *punāmy acchidreṇa*]; *vājjy arvā* [becomes *vājy arvā*]; *vettv ājyasya* [becomes *vettv ājyasya*]; *vibhūr mātrā prabhūḥ pitrā* [becomes *vibhūr mātrā prabhūḥ pitrā*]. There is no example of the vowel *lṛ* in the *saṃhitā*. Regarding the diphthongs (*sandhyakṣara*), [the rule states]: "They become *aya*, *ava*, and *āva*. (Pāṇini 6.1.78).

The vowels known as *sandhakṣara*—namely *e*, *o*, *ai*, and *au*—undergo these substitutions (*ay*, *av*, *āy*, *āv*) when followed by another vowel; for example, in *iḍa ehi*. Once the substitution *ay* has been made, there is elision of *y* and *v* when they occur at the end of a word and are situated between vowels.

When two vowels exist between them, there is the elision (*lopa*) of the *y* and *v* sounds that stand at the end of a word (*padānta*). In the case of *sarasvatyā indrāya* and *viṣṇo ete*, once the substitution of *ava* has been made and the elision would have been applicable by the preceding rule (*pūrvasūtra*), a prohibition is made by the following rule. "According to some, there is no elision of the *v* sound at the end of a word when it stands between two vowels in different places (*asasthāna*). Thus, for the *v* sound at the end of a word situated between two vowels in different places, there is no elision when a vowel of a different place of articulation (*bhinnasthāna*) follows, as in *viṣṇavete*. [Examples include] *ānanda-nandau-aṇḍau*.

What is meant by "in an improper place" (asasthāna)? [Example: *viṣṇo urugāya*. The two *ūr* are said to be the feet. 7. Before a guttural vowel (*kaṇṭhya*) followed by the vowel *ṛ*, a short vowel becomes [the single substitute]. [Example: *tva ṛbhumate*. 8. When a similar vowel (*savarṇa*) follows, a long vowel [becomes the single substitute]. [Example: *siṛtha*.

A vowel termed *siṃ* (a short vowel), when followed by a homogeneous vowel (*savarṇa*), undergoes a single long substitution for both the preceding and the following vowel. For example: *nārātaye*, *svāhāgnaye*, *yaumīdam*, *pacantūṣe*. Here, although the rule "before a vowel, [the preceding vowel becomes] a semivowel" would have applied, this very rule takes effect by virtue of being subsequent, according to the principle of "conflict" (*vipratiṣedha*). 9. A vowel of the guttural class (*kaṇṭhya*) followed by the vowel *i*, with the vowel *i* preceding it, undergoes a single substitution of *e*. For example: *jayendrāya*, *edam*. 10. [A vowel of the guttural class followed by] the vowel *u*, with the vowel *u* preceding it, undergoes a single substitution of *o*. For example: *uṣe*.
An *u*-vowel following a guttural and the preceding [guttural] become a single *o* sound. For example: *ihorjjam* and *prohāmi*. The diphthongs are *ai* and *au*. 11.

When preceded by a guttural vowel, these two—*aikāra* and *aukāra*—undergo the substitution of the diphthongs (*sandhyakṣara*). For example: *bhrājāyaiṣa te*, *indreṇaindram*, *ojiṣṭhaujiṣṭhaḥ*, *praukṣan*, and *samudrasyemaṃstvemaṃstvodmann*. These are established as exceptions (*nipātana*). An exception (*nipātana*) is the pronunciation of something in one way when it would otherwise have been obtained in another. As in: *apāṃ pṛṣṭhe samudrasyeman*, *apāntveman*, and *apāntvodman*. [Furthermore,] that which belongs to a later time [is not applied] when there is a prior time. 12.

A rule that occurs later (parakāla) is superseded by a rule that occurs earlier (pūrvakāla); when the earlier rule has been applied, the later rule becomes established as non-existent. Let them hear this here: the two examples are cited. [In the cases of] *arādhyā edidhiṣuḥpatim* and *rātryā ṛkṣaḥ*, because the rule "of the two *y* and *v* sounds at the end of a word" (*yavayoḥ padāntayoḥ*) is a later rule, once it has arisen, the euphonic operation (saṃdhi-kārya) that was applicable according to its respective rule at the earlier stage does not take place. [The following is the exception: "An *ṛ*-vowel [is substituted] after an uncombined vowel (*apṛkta*). (Pāṇini 6.1.13).

An *ṛ*-sound following an uncombined (*apṛkta*) vowel, as well as the preceding vowel, undergoes a single substitution. This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the rule that an *ṛ*-sound is produced from a guttural (*kaṇṭhya*). That which is prescribed when something else is necessarily applicable is an exception to that, just as the rule for *svapanam* is an exception to the rule for *ārtyai*. [The preceding vowel] becomes *a* after *e* and *o*. 14.

The letter *a* following *e* or *o*, as well as the preceding [vowel], becomes a single *e* or *o*. In this section, for those words ending in a visarga, when the rule "all [the vowels] become *o*" is being followed, the state of ending in *o* is established by the two subsequent sūtras beginning with "if there is an *a*. An example is: *agnaye'nīkavate*; *agnerdabdhāyo'śītama*. In the case of the Ṛgvedic verses, there is the preservation of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*).

In the *ṛc* verses—those mantras characterized by fixed syllables and meters—an *a* that follows *e* or *o* remains in its original form (*prakṛti*). This is an exception to the rule concerning *e* and *o*. For example: *garbhe'ntaḥ* and *vāyo'smin*. And this also applies in the *yajus* formulas. 16.

In the case of indeterminate syllables, without distinction, an *a* following the sounds *e* and *o*, as well as the preceding *a*, becomes *e* or *o*. For example: *agrepuvo 'gre*; *ca me 'pānaḥ*. Because of the word "and" (*ca*), this also occurs occasionally in *ṛk* verses: *yo 'sāv āditye puruṣaḥ so 'sāv aham*; *kā dhruvītī sadanā*; *hotārā jyā*; *svadhā pṛthivī*; *pratimemasadann aśyāmākarma*; *ūrdhvam iyam avastād utāstiṣu*. 17.

The nine words beginning with *kā* remain in their original form (*prakṛti*) when followed by these nine subsequent words respectively: *kā īm*, *dhruvā asadat*, *ūtī aśyām*, *sadanā akarma*, *hotārā ūrdhvam*, *jyā iyam*, *svadhā avastāt*, *pṛthivī uta dyauḥ*, *pratimā asti*. 18. A word designated as *pragṛhya* remains in its original form when followed by a vowel. Examples: *indrāgnī apāt*, *indravāyū ime*, *śipre avepayaḥ*, *asmme ārāt*, *tve iṣaḥ*, *amī agnyaḥ*. 19. The letter *u*, when not joined in conjunction (*apṛkta*), remains in its original form when followed by a non-contact consonant (*aspṛśat*). Examples: *uta*, *upari*.

The preceding statement is for the purpose of restriction regarding the existence [of the vowel]: an *apṛkta* vowel *u* remains in its original form (*prakṛtyā*) only when it does not follow a *sparśa* (stop). For example: *etavā u añji*. Why "not following a *sparśa*"? As in: *taddvantike*, *samvetaddadhāmi*, *na rodasīme*.

The dual-ending word *rodasī* also does not remain in its original form when followed by these words: *ime*, *śabde*, *pare*, *a*, *rodasī*, *me*, *ṇye*. Thus, the eight vowels have been explained along with their examples. Now, the objects to be demonstrated by means of the fingers will be explained. In that regard, these properties belong to the consonants; for this reason, the conjunction of consonants (*vyañjana-saṃdhi*) is stated first. The group of *t*-sounds [is merged] into the group of *c*-sounds, and the group of *c*-sounds... [into the group of *k*-sounds]. 1.

The five consonants beginning with *t* (the *tavarga*) become the five consonants beginning with *c* (the *cavarga*) when followed by any one of the consonants beginning with *c*. Here, the correspondence between the substituends (*sthānin*) and the substitutes (*ādeśa*) is according to their respective order; however, this does not apply to the rule "before *ś*" (*śakāre ca*), because that rule is a supplement to the present sūtra and thus has six causes (*nimitta*). The division of the yoga (*yogavibhāga*) is for the purpose of carrying [the rule] forward into the subsequent sūtra. Furthermore: *āccha chandaḥ*; *anūjjeṣam*; *śatrūñ jayatu*. When followed by *ś*, and also when followed by *ś*, the *tavarga* becomes the *cavarga*. As in: *adityāñ śmaśrubhiḥ*. And when followed by a non-aspirate (*asparśa*), it becomes *ch*: *paraś chāsparśaparaś chām*.

A *ś* following the *tavarga* (the dental class) becomes *ch*, provided it is not followed by a *sparśa* (stop consonant). A *c* preceding a *t* becomes the *cavarga* (the palatal class). As in *yacchuddhe* and *kūśmāñchakapiṇḍaiḥ*. Why "not followed by a *sparśa*"? To understand this, one should refer to the examples from the previous rule. *Nuḥ*: 4. This is a governing heading (*adhikāra*). *Anunāsikam upadhā*: 5. This also functions in the same way. *Ca chayoh śam*: 6. [A *ś* following *c* or *ch* becomes *ś*].

When *ca* or *cha* follows, *na* becomes *śa*, and the preceding vowel (*upadhā*) becomes nasalized (*anunāsika*). Examples: *tāṃścakkre*; in *jaṭā*, *avaṃśchantsi*. Likewise, when *ta* or *tha* follow, *na* becomes *sa*, and the preceding vowel becomes nasalized. Examples: *aśmmaṃste*; *paśūṃstān*. When *ya* follows, *dadhannvāntsvavān* undergoes elision (*lopa*).

In these two cases, the letter *n* undergoes elision when followed by the letter *y*. There is no nasalization (*anunāsika*) of the preceding vowel here. And it is stated in the *Vasiṣṭhaśikṣā*: "They always acknowledge the nasalization of vowels, with the exception of that *ā* where elision is prescribed. Examples: *dadhannvā yaḥ*; *svavāyātu*; *rayivṛdhe ca*. When *rayivṛdhaḥ* follows, the letter *n* undergoes elision. Example: *pīvo'nnā rayivṛdhaḥ*. When *pakāra* follows, the *ṇ* becomes a *visarjanīya*. Example: *nṝnpakāre*.

The *nakāra* (the letter *n*) in the words *nṛ*, *ṇṛ*, *nitya*, and *arthaṃ* becomes a *visarjanīya* when followed by the letter *p*. The preceding vowel (*upadhā*) also becomes nasalized (*anunāsika*). Examples: *nṛm̐ pāhi* (protect men), *śatrūn paridhīn kratūn vanaspatīn* (enemies, enclosures, rites, and trees).

In these [words], the *nakāra* becomes a *repha* (the sound *r*) when followed by a vowel. The preceding vowel also becomes nasalized. Examples: *śatrū r apa* (away from enemies), *paridhī m̐* (enclosures), *rapo ṛṇu* (remove sin), *kratūṃ r anu* (according to the rites). For it has been stated by Pārāśara that "these [nasalized vowels] consist of one half-mora (*ardhamātrā*). When preceded by the vowel *ā*, [the *nakāra*] becomes a *yakāra* (the sound *y*). 12.

The letter *na*, when followed by the vowel *ā* as its *upadhā* (penultimate), becomes *ya* before a vowel, and the *upadhā* becomes nasalized (*anunāsika*). As in *yām* and *āvahaḥ*. Here, even though there is elision (*lopa*) of *ya* and *va* by the rule "of *ya* and *va*," the subsequent [operation] does not apply to the preceding due to the principle "what is later is not effective for what is earlier," and because it belongs to a different section, the exclusion of the nasalized form does not occur. A contact consonant (*sparśa*), other than the fifth [class], [becomes] the third [consonant of its class] before a vowel.

In each class of consonants, when followed by a vowel or a letter belonging to the *dhi* group (the sibilants and *h*), the first letter of that class becomes the third letter of its own class. Examples of this transition: *ṛdhag ityā*, *reḍ asi*, *tad id āsaṃ*. An example from the *Saṅkrama* [section]: *anuṣṭub evaḥ*, *ūrg asi*, *rāḍ yantrī*, *tasmād yajñāt*, *triṣṭub jagatī*. Why "not the fifth"? [As in: *yuṅ asi*, *asmin yajñe*. 14. A non-fifth contact consonant (*sparśa*) becomes the fifth contact consonant of its own class when followed by a fifth contact consonant. Example: *vāk māttyā* becomes *vvāṅ māttyā*. *yan me chidram*. 15. And when followed by *ha*, the fourth letter of the preceding class [becomes the fifth]. Example: *yan me chidram* becomes *yan mme chidram*. *haś ca tasmāt pūrvacaturtham*.

A *hakāra* (the letter *h*) that follows a consonant other than the fifth [class-consonant] becomes the fourth [consonant] of the preceding [class], and the *cakāra* (*c*) that precedes it becomes the third [consonant]. Examples: *vvāgghutaḥ*, *samasusroddhṛdaḥ*, *avāḍḍhavvyāni*. Why "not after the fifth"? [Counter-example: *jīmūtāghṛdayaupaśena*. In the presence of *anusvāra*, *ṭha*, *ra*, and *ṣma*, the *makāra* [becomes the nasal of its own class]. 16.

The letter *ma* becomes an *anusvāra* when followed by the sibilants (*ūṣman*) or the letter *ra*. For that *anusvāra*, there is a substitution (*ādeśa*) with *ṛ*, *ṭ*, *ṛ*, *ṣ*, *ś*, *s*, *ha*, or *ra*. Yājñavalkya has demonstrated the manner of forming these—the *anusvāra* and the others—with the fingers: "In the case of *ma*, the form is that of a fist; in the case of *na*, it is the grasping of the fingernails. At the end of *ka* and at the end of *ṭa*, for *ṅa* and *ṇa*, there is the bending down of the fingers. In the case of *pa*, it is five fingers; in the case of *ta*, it is the shape of an earring (*kuṇḍala*). That which arises from an upward throw is the *ūṣman*; and that which arises from a downward throw [is the *anusvāra*]."

The wise man should release [the fingers] one by one; however, when there is a *svarita* accent, he should release both. Whatever *svarita* occurs, whether it be accompanied by a *vakra*, a sibilant (*ūṣman*), or whether it be long or short, there is a release of both.
If a *yakāra* is seen in both a *jātya* and a *svarita* accent, then according to the view of the Vāyavyas, a release of both must be performed.

Likewise, in the *Laghu-mādhyandinīya-śikṣā*: "One should perform the release of the little finger when there is a low tone (*nīca*) and a *pracaya* accent; the first [finger] for *namaḥ kūpyāya*, and likewise the second for *jāgrataḥ*."

One should perform the *tarjanīmocana* (finger-release) gesture upon an acute (*udātta*) vowel, but the release of the fingers (*visargaka*) upon a grave (*anudātta*). In the case of a short circumflex (*hrasve svarite*), one should likewise [perform the release]; however, in the long circumflex (*svarite*), one should cast both [fingers].

The horse becomes mortal as the target when there is a long *svāra* (circumflex); in the case of a short *vakāra* (the letter *va*) that is circumflexed, it applies to both [long and short vowels]. 3.

Furthermore, the established rule of the Śāstra is that for both [the long vowel and the consonant], there is a simultaneous movement. For this [sound], the asterism is *arkṣa*. At the letter *ma*, it is the fist. At the letter *na*, one grasps the nail of the index finger with the thumb. At the letters *ka*, *ṭa*, *ṅa*, and *ṇa*—as well as in the *padapāṭha* of words such as *vṛṣaṇvasu* and others—one should bend the index finger downward. At the letter *pa*, there is the joining of the five fingers. At the letter *ta*, it takes the shape of a coil (*kuṇḍala*). These modes apply everywhere at the end of words. When a *visarga* follows an *udātta* vowel, there is the extension of the index finger.

The spreading of the little finger occurs after an unaccented vowel (*anudātta*) and after a protracted vowel (*pracaya*). The spreading of both the index and little fingers occurs after a short *svarita* vowel. After a long *svarita* vowel followed by a *visarga*, there is a movement of the little finger. This also applies to both [fingers] after a long vowel joined with the letter *va*. It likewise applies to both after a long vowel joined with the letter *ya* that is a *jātya-svarita*. Thus, the objects indicated by the fingers have been described. Now, the object concerning the *anusvāra* is explained.
In the presence of *repha* (r) and the sibilants (*ūṣman*), the letter *m* becomes an *anusvāra*.

That is, the letter *m* undergoes the change to *anusvāra* when followed by *repha* or the sibilants. For example: *apām rasena* [becomes] *apāṃrasena*; *tvām* [becomes] *tvaṃ*; *śaśvantaḥ* [becomes] *śaśvaṃtaḥ*; *devam savitāram* [becomes] *devarṭha0 savitāram*; *urum hi* [becomes] *ururṭha0 hi*. And so it is stated in the *Pratijñāsūtra*:

The *anusvāra* is substituted by *ṛt* (ṛ, ṭ, ṭh) when followed by the letters *ś*, *ṣ*, *s*, *h*, or *r*. Its threefold nature is explained through the distinctions of short (*hrasva*), long (*dīrgha*), and heavy (*guru*). A short vowel following a long vowel becomes long; a long vowel following a short vowel becomes long; and [a vowel] following a heavy consonant becomes heavy. In the place of the *anusvāra*, the substitute *ṛt* occurs when *ś*, *ṣ*, *s*, *h*, or *r* follows—this is the remainder of the rule. For example: *triṛśat*, *havīṃṣi*, *payāṃsi*, *dṛṛhasva*, *saṛrāyaḥ*. From a short syllable, a long vowel [is produced].

When a heavy syllable (*guru*) is followed by another heavy syllable, or when a conjunct consonant (*saṃyuktākṣara*) follows, the preceding syllable becomes heavy. Examples in order: A short vowel followed by a long vowel, as in: *pṛthivyāmaṃśatena*, *yajūṃṣi*, *sasṛvāṃsam*, *aṅktāṃ haviṣā*, *iṣāṃ rayīṇām*. A long vowel followed by a short vowel, as in: *triḥ ṣaddhāma*, *sarvaḥ ṣaḍiti*, *bhūyāḥ su-gṛhapatiḥ*, *sa rāyas-poṣeṇa*. A heavy syllable followed by another heavy syllable, as in: *bheṣajaṃ śriyā*, *daṃṣṭrābhyām*.

*Somānaṃ svaraṇam*. You are a lioness (*siṃhī asi*). When followed by a conjunction with the letter *ṛ*, there is only a long vowel (*dīrgha*) and not a heavy syllable (*guru*). And it is stated in the *Kātyāyana-śikṣā*: "In Vedic usage, the substitution of the letter *ṛ* for the *anusvāra* is prescribed. When followed by sibilants (*ūṣman*) or the letter *r*, its threefold nature is declared: [the *anusvāra* becomes] long after a short [vowel], short after a long [vowel], and heavy when followed by a heavy [syllable]. A sibilant ending in *ṛ* (i.e., *ṛt*), even after a long [vowel], becomes long."*1* 1. *Somānaṃ svaraṇam* (RV 9.1.6): "O Soma, you are the one who makes us hear our songs. *siṃhyasi* (TS 4.1.2.1): "You are a lioness. In these cases, because the *anusvāra* is replaced by *ṛ*, the preceding vowel remains long, yet the syllable does not become heavy due to the specific phonetic rules governing this substitution. As the *Śikṣā* explains, the resulting sound is determined by the following consonant: it is long after a short vowel, short after a long vowel, and heavy when followed by a heavy syllable. Furthermore, when a sibilant follows an *ṛ*-sound, even if it occurs after a long vowel, it results in a long vowel. Thus, in *somānam* and *siṃhyasi*, the *anusvāra* is replaced by *ṛ*, and the vowel maintains its length according to these rules.

And likewise, in the *Amoghanandinī-śikṣā*: "The *anusvāra* shall have two morae (*mātrā*) when followed by a vowel or a consonant, whether after a short or a long [vowel], as in *devānārṭha* and *hṛdaye*. In the case of a conjunct consonant (*saṃyoga*), a short [mora] is prescribed, as in *sarṭha*sṛṣṭajit and *sarṭha*sṛṣṭām. This is the rule regarding the *anusvāra*. Now follows the consideration of the display of fingers (*aṅgulipradarśana*) for the *anusvāra*. And so it is stated in the *Sarvasaṅgraha-hastasvara-prakriyā* composed by Mallakavi: "In the case of a long [vowel], the index finger (*deśinī*) should be withdrawn; it should be done quickly for a double [consonant], and lightly for a single [consonant]."

The meaning of this is as follows: because it occurs in the section concerning the *anusvāra*, when there is a long *anusvāra*, the *deśinī* (the ring finger) and the *pradeśinī* (the middle finger) are to be abandoned—that is, they should be withdrawn. When there is a double-marked *anusvāra*, whether heavy (*guru*) or light (*laghu*)—that is, short (*hrasva*)—it should be performed quickly. "Quickly" (*kṣipram*) is indeed described in the *Agnimakārikā*: "With the thumb joined to the back of the index finger and its tip bent forward—one should recognize that as 'quick,' as declared by those who know the vowels. (5)

This is the intended meaning: whether the *anusvāra* is short or long, the back of the index finger must be bent by the tip of the thumb. Having stated this generally as "the casting of the finger upon the *anusvāra*," it is further specified: "In the case of a short *anusvāra*, there is a contraction of the thumb; in the case of a long one, the extension of the index finger is proclaimed. (6)

Thus, this [practice] appears to be consistent with the scripture propounded by the venerable Yājñavalkya, which states: "In the case of a long *anusvāra* and the letter *ra*, there is the extension of the index finger; in other cases—namely, a short *anusvāra* and a *guru* [heavy] *anusvāra*—there is the contraction of the thumb. However, the contraction of the index finger occurs because there is no sublation [of that rule] and because it is specifically prescribed. For this very reason, even learned scholars extend the index finger for a long *anusvāra*; for a light (*laghu*) or heavy (*guru*) *anusvāra*, they bend the thumb onto the back of the index finger.
Regarding the *sparśa* [consonants], [the rule is] "the fifth of the subsequent [class]. 3.

The letter *m* becomes the fifth [consonant] of the following class when followed by a contact consonant (*sparśa*). Examples such as *hiṅkārāya*, *ahaṅkhanāmi*, and *iṣuṅgiriśante* should be understood. 4. Regarding the *parasavarṇa* [substitution], there is a slight modification of the original form (*prakṛtyā*): one should pronounce something slightly similar to the following sound. 5. When a semivowel (*antasthā*) is followed by another semivowel, it becomes a nasalized semivowel (*anunāsikām antasthām*) that shares the same place of articulation (*samānasthāna*) as the following one. Examples: *taṃyyajñam*, *saṃvvapāmi*, *taṃllokam*. 6. The letter *t* becomes *l* before *l*.
The letter *ta* becomes *la* when followed by *la*. As in: *āsīllokam*, *paricillokam*. Rule 7:

When *na* is followed by *la*, it becomes the nasalized (*anunāsika*) *la*. As in: *asmiṃlloke*, *trīṃllokān*. Rule 8: A vowel before a *cha* or a *ca* is everywhere replaced by *ca* as an augment. This is prescribed at the beginning, middle, or end of a word. As in: *acchāvadāmasi*, *mācchandaḥ*, *jagatīcchandaḥ*. Rule 9: [This rule applies] where there is *ati*, *hā*, or *ayasa*; [otherwise] not.
Not for these [words]: *sahachandasaḥ*, *atihāyachidrā*, and *yasya chāyā*. Regarding the rule *ṅnau ktābhyāṃ sakāre*:

when the suffixes *ṅ* and *n* follow the roots *kṛ* and *tṛ* respectively, they are separated from the following *sakāra* by the letters *ka* and *ta*. For example: *prāṅṅaksomaḥ* (from *prāṅ + ṅak + somaḥ*) and *samuddrāntsamasṛpat* (from *samudra + ant + samasṛpat*). Regarding the rule *udastabhāne lopam*: [the *ṅ*] is elided before *udasta*. For example: *udastabhāne*.

The *s* of the word *stabhāna*, when preceded by *udaḥ*, becomes *ṣ*. For example: *uttambhāna*. This is because the rule "of that which follows" (*tasmād ity uttarasyādeḥ*) specifies that the change applies to what is immediately contiguous. Therefore, in the case of *uddivaṃstabhāna*, the elision of the *s* does not occur. Furthermore, when a *cari* (a sibilant) follows a vowel that is to undergo modification (*bhāvya*), and the following *visarjanīya* is followed by *r*, the *visarjanīya* is elided and the preceding vowel is lengthened. (12)

When a *visarga* preceded by a short vowel (*upadha*) and followed by a *repha* (the letter *r*), it is elided and the preceding *upadha* becomes long. Examples from the *Jaṭā*: *vvasubhīruddraiḥ*, *antārukkmaḥ*, *nīrapāṃsi*, *rurūraudraḥ*, *dhātūrāyaḥ*. [The rule continues: "A *repha* [is inserted] before a vowel or the letter *dh*. (13)

A *visarga* that is preceded by a *bhāvyupadha* (a vowel other than *a*) and followed by a *riphita* vowel or a consonant belonging to the *dhi*-class, undergoes the substitution of *repha* (*r*). Examples: *pṛśnir akramīt*, *vāyur anilam*, *agnir mūrdhā*, *tvaṣṭur jāmātaḥ*, *aharjin nva*. [This is so] because it has been stated [in the rule] that [the *visarga*] is not followed by the letter *bha* (i.e., *bh*, *gh*, *j*, *jh*, *ñ*; *kh*, *ch*, *th*, *th*, *ṭh*; *ph*, *chh*, *ṭh*, *ṭh*, *kṣ*). Examples: *śuddhyatu śamaho bhyah*, *svardyor iva*. [This is so] because it has been stated that [the *visarga*] is at the beginning of a word and is not followed by a non-*ji* vowel (i.e., *a*, *ā*, *i*, *ī*, *u*, *ū*, *ṛ*, *ṝ*, *ḷ*, *e*, *ai*, *o*, *au*). Examples: *svargyāya*, *anaraṇe*. [This is so] because it has been stated [in the rule] "and for *sva* and *caraṇa*," [providing an exception]. This is a prohibition of what was otherwise applicable due to being followed by a non-*ji* vowel.

A *visarga* preceded by a guttural (*kaṇṭhya*) and not followed by a *riphita* letter becomes *y*, provided it is not separated from the *riphita* [by another sound], when followed by a vowel. For example: *ya imā viśvā* (from *yaḥ imā*), *śuṣmā oṣadhīnām* (from *śuṣmaḥ oṣadhīnām*). There is elision according to the rule *yavayoḥ*. Elision occurs before a *dh* sound.

A non-*ariphita* visarga preceded by a guttural vowel becomes *sopadha* (retains its *u*-element) when followed by the case-ending *dhau*. For example: *devāḥ* becomes *devāḥ*; *ayakṣmāḥ* becomes *ayakṣmā mā*. 16. The visarga associated with the word *bhūmi* undergoes elision (*lopa*) when followed by an uncombined (*apṛkta*) vowel *a*. For example: *bhūmyādade*. 17. A non-*ariphita* visarga preceded by a short *a* vowel becomes *okāra* (the sound *o*), provided it has an *u*-element (*sopadha*), when followed by the case-ending *dhau*. This is an exception to the rule of elision (*lopaṃ dhau*). For example: *devaḥ* becomes *devau*; *devaḥ* becomes *devau*; *devaḥ* becomes *devau* [in the sense of] "O gods, may Savitṛ be for you. 18. And [it becomes *o*] when followed by the vowel *a*. For example: *devaḥ* becomes *devo*.

A *visarga* preceded by a short vowel from the *kaṇṭhya* (velar) class, when followed by an *a*-vowel, becomes *o*, provided it is preceded by another vowel. For example: *stupo 'si* and *kṛṣṇo 'si*. *Sva-ruha-* and *aha-* become *o* before the word *rātri*.

That is, the word *svaḥ* becomes *svo* before *ruha-*, and the word *ahaḥ* becomes *aho* before the word *rātri*. For example: *svoruhāṇāḥ* and *ahorātrayoḥ*. Before *ca* and *cha*, the *visarga* becomes *ś*. For example: *indraśca* and *prajāpatiśchandaḥ*. Similarly, before *ta* and *tha*, [the *visarga* becomes *ṣ*]. For example: *indraṣṭhāḥ* and *prajāpatiṣṭhāḥ*.
The *visarga* is likewise assimilated before *tha* and *ya*: *kastvā*, *namaste*. According to Śākalya, there is no modification before *ṭha*, *śa*, *ṣa*, and *sa*. (Pāṇini 8.3.19–22)

In these cases, according to the opinion of Śākalya, the *visarga* does not undergo modification. [Examples: *vāyavyāḥ śvetāḥ*; *agnīṣomayoḥ ṣaṣṭhī*; *vānaspatyāḥ*. 23. Before *ka*, *kha*, *pa*, and *pha*, the *visarga* remains in its original form (*prakṛtyā*). [Examples: *simāḥ kṛṇvanti*; *tataḥ khanema*; *vasoḥ pavitram*; *yāḥ phalinoḥ*. 24. Among the Mādhyandinas, the *la-lha*, *jihvāmūlīya*, *upadhmānīya*, and *nāsikya* do not exist. Thus, the prohibitions established by the Pāṇinian sūtras should be understood here. 25. When followed by a letter with the marker *j* (a sibilant), the *luṃ-mud* (the nasalization) occurs.
The *visarga* is elided when followed by a sound belonging to the *mut* class or the *am* class. *amṛtāstutāḥ* (amṛta-astutāḥ). *ūrjjastya* (ūrja-asty-a). 26. *pīvaḥ*:
This *visarga* is elided when followed by the word *upavasana*. *pīvopavasanānām* (pīva-upavasanānām). 27. *sa oṣadhīmayoḥ*:

The *visarga* represented by "sa" is elided when followed by the words *oṣadhī* or *ima*. *sauṣadhīranu* (sa-oṣadhīranu). *semānnaḥ* (sa-imānnaḥ). 28. *vyañjane ca*: [The *visarga* is elided] also before a consonant.

This *visarga* following *sa-* is elided when followed by a consonant. Examples: *sa te lokaḥ*, *sa paryagāt*, *sa bodhi*. *Sya* and *eṣa*: these two *visargas* are elided when followed by a consonant. Examples: *sya rāttyaḥ*, *eṣate*, *eṣacchāgaḥ*. *Sya vājī*, *eṣasya*. These two rules (*sūtras*) indicate the application of *sam* and so forth to *ta-tha*.

In cases such as *sya vājī* and *sa bodhi*, the rule "every *a*-sound becomes *o*" sets aside preceding rules but not subsequent ones; thus, by the principle of conflict (*vipratiṣedha*), the subsequent [rule] is stronger, provided there is no elision (*alopa*). 30.

Because this has been stated, its sublation was initially considered an intermediate exception (*madhye'pavāda*); however, because it has been stated that there is no elision (*alopa*), it does not occur. [End of Chapter 31] on *anit*.

This is a governing rule (*adhikāra*). An operation consisting of an augment (*āgama*), a modification (*vikāra*), and so forth, which is being prescribed, does not take place when followed by *i*, *t*, or *u*. This is because [the rule] "except for *upasthita*" is impossible in this context due to its being subsequent. However, since the *sthitopasthita* (the rule that remains and applies again) has the same scope, this prohibition concerns modifications and augments within a word (*pada*). The governing rule "in a chapter" (*adhyāye*) is for the purpose of defining its limit. Why is it a governing rule? Consider *tavastaram*: from *tavaḥ* and *taram*, the rule beginning with "when *sa* follows *ta* and *tha*" (*tathayoḥ saḥ*) would otherwise apply. Why "in a chapter"? Consider *govyaccham*: from *go* and *vyaccham*.

In such cases as these, when there is a vowel [following], *bhāvī* and so forth occurs. This prohibition applies only to a word that possesses a modification (*vikāra*), by virtue of the principle of "standing and rising" (*sthitopasthita*); therefore, in the case of *rāyaspoṣada*, [the form] is *rāyaspoṣa*. Here, in the phrase *rāyaḥ sahasaḥ*, the *s*-sound occurs. Thus, regarding the *carccā* (repetition): 32. *Carccā* is that which is uttered again. Just as a word following an *iti* does not occur when another *iti* follows, so it is here. 33. The *s*-sound [occurs] for *k* and *p*. 34. When followed by a sound to be modified (*bhāvī*), the *ṣ*-sound [occurs].

A visarga followed by a labial vowel (*bhāvyupadha*) becomes *ṣ*. By elimination, a *s* preceded by a guttural (*kaṇṭhya*) becomes *ṣ* when followed by a *k*. This is a governing rule (*adhikāra*). In the subsequent sūtras, both [rules] apply as appropriate. 35. In the words *āvis*, *niriḍa*, *iḍāyāḥ*, *vasatiḥ*, and *varivaḥ*, the visarga becomes *s* or *ṣ* respectively before *k* and *p*. Examples: *āviṣkṛṇuṣva*, *ambaniṣppara*, *iḍasppade*, *iḍāyāsppadam*, *vasatiṣkṛtā*, *varivaskṛṇotu*. 36. [The visarga of] *divaḥ* becomes *ṣ* before *kakud* and *pṛthivī*. Example: *divasppṛthivyāḥ*. (Note: *kakut* is understood from the previous rule.)

This *visarga* following the word *div-* becomes *s* before the letters *k* and *p*, with the exception of the words *kakud* and *pṛthivī*. Examples: *divas pari*, *divas putrāya*, *divas pṛṣṭhe*. Why "not before *kakud*" and so forth? [Counter-examples: *divaḥ kakud*, *divaḥ pṛthivyāḥ*. [Rule 37: The *visarga* of *rāyaḥ* and *sahasas* becomes *s* before *poṣa* and *putra*.

These two [visargas] become *sakāra* (s) respectively before the words *poṣa* and *putra* when they follow. Examples: *rāyasppoṣe*; *sahasasppuśnaḥ*. 38. This visarga becomes *sakāra* before the words *kapa* and *para*, with the exception of the word *parastāt*. Examples: *tamasasppari*. Why "before *apara*"? As in: *tamasaḥ parastāt*. Example: *tamasaspṛthivvyām*. 39. This [visarga] becomes *sakāra* before the word *pṛthivī*. Example: *tapasaspṛthivvyām*. 40. [The visarga becomes *sakāra*] before the words *adhvanaḥ*, *rajasaḥ*, *riṣaḥ*, and *spṛśaḥ*, as well as before the word *pātu*. Examples: *adhvanspātau*, *rajanspātau*, *riṣanspātau*, *spṛśanspātau*.

These four [words] undergo the substitution of *s* for *ṣ* in the Prāg-dhātuka [affixes]: *addhvanaspātu*, *rajasaspāti*, *riṣaspāhi*, and *saṃspṛśaspāhi*. Furthermore, the form *addhvanaskuru* is also derived by this rule;
it is an irregular formation (*nipātana*) where *sakam* [is substituted]. Thus: *addhvanaskuru*. And [this applies] within a single word (*samānapade*). 42.

A *visarga* occurring in a single word becomes a *sakāra* (s) or a *ṣakāra* (ṣ), as appropriate, when followed by *ka* or *pa*, provided that *itaḥ* does not follow and this occurs within the scope of *carca* (repetition). It does not occur otherwise. Examples: *śreyaskara* (from *śreyaḥ-kara*) *tapaspatiḥ* (from *tapaḥ-patiḥ*) *haviṣkṛt* (from *haviḥ-kṛt*) *catuṣpāt* (from *catuḥ-pāt*) In the case of *sthitopasthita* (the repetition of a word): *śreyaḥ kareti śreyaḥ kara* (from *śreyaḥ-kara*) *tapaḥ patiriti tapaḥ patiḥ* (from *tapaḥ-patiḥ*) *jāḥpattyamiti jāḥ pattyam* (from *jāḥ-pattyam*) *haviṣkṛditi haviḥ kṛt* (from *haviḥ-kṛt*) *catuṣpāditi catuḥ pāt* (from *catuḥ-pāt*) And so forth. [Rule 43: *parāvavasāne* (at the end of a sentence).

When the word *pari* stands at the end of a phrase (*avasāna*) and follows [a vowel], it becomes *visarga*. For example: *oṣadhayas pari*. Why "at the end of a phrase"? Consider: *heḍaḥ pari te vṛṇaktu*. In the presence of the words *kaviḥ*, *karat*, and *kṛdhi*, the *visarga* undergoes the change to *sakāra* (s) or *ṣakāra* (ṣ). For example: *vasuṣkaviḥ*; *śreyasaskarat*; *punaskṛdhi*. And in the case of *kṛṣi*, there is *sakāra* before the word *kṛdhi*. For example: *punaskṛdhi*.

The *visarga* of the word *kṛṣi* becomes *sakāra* (*s*) before the word *kṛdhi*. Since the preceding rule would have required it to become *ṣakāra* due to the following vowel being a "future" (*bhāvī*) *upadhā*, this specific injunction is made. Thus: *kṛṣīskṛdhi*. Regarding the words *sadaḥ*, *dyauḥ*, and *namaskṛtam* before the words *pitā* and *patheṣu*: the *visarga* of these three becomes *saṃ* or *ṣaṃ* respectively before *kṛtam* and so forth. Examples: *yeṣām apsu sadaskṛtam*; *upahūto dyauṣpitā*; *śarmma sapprathā namaspathe*. And [the *visarga*] becomes *saṃ* when followed by a word beginning with a palatal (*tālavya*) vowel. (47)

When the word *pati* follows a palatal vowel (*tālavya-svara*) at the end of a word-form (*pada-rūpa*), the *visarga* becomes *sakāra*. The phrase "preceded by a palatal vowel" (*tālavya-svare-udaya*) is intended to include the opinion of Sāṃmya. Examples: *brahmaṇasppate*, *vācasppataye*, *vācasppatim*. Why say "in a word-form" (*pade*)? [Because the rule applies when the preceding sound is part of a word. The mention of the locative case in "indicated as being in that" (*tasminn iti nirdiṣṭe*) refers to a situation where a specific phoneme is indicated by its position within a word. In this context, this very point serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*), because it is impossible for a sound separated from a word-part to be so indicated. Example: *yato jātaḥ prajāpatiḥ*. [The following rule applies: "Not in the case of *paruṣaḥ paruṣi*" (48).

This *visarga* in the word *paruṣa* does not become *sakāra* before *paruṣi*. This is a prohibition of what was previously established by the rule "when within the same word" (*samānapade*). Examples: *prarohantī paruṣaḥ paruṣaḥ*; *vājapatiḥ*, *vāsaḥ*, *edidhiṣuḥ*, *antaḥparśavyena*, and *antaḥpārśvyam*. (49)

In the three [mantras] beginning with *kapayoḥ vājapatiḥ*, the elision (*visarga*) and the connection with the two words beginning with *antaḥ parśavyena* do not undergo modification. There is a prohibition against [the application of] *vājapatiḥ kaviḥ kaviḥ karat*. [The forms] *vāsaḥ palppūlīm*, *edidhiṣuḥ patim*, and *antaḥ parśavyena* (which becomes *antaḥ pārśvyam*) involve a prohibition of what was otherwise obtained by the rule *samānapade ca*. The phrase *iti ca* serves the purpose of an inclusive collection (*anuktasamuccaya*); therefore, there is no *sakāra* in *jātaḥ patiḥ*. [In the case of] *ahaḥ patau*, there is a *repha*. 50.

The word *ahar*, when followed by the word *pati*, undergoes the change to the letter *r*. This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the rule regarding "the same word" (*samānapada*). Example: *aharpataye*. However, in the case of *sthitopasthita* (where the two words are separated by an avagraha), it remains as *ahaḥ pataye*. "Subsequent" (*paraśca*) and "cerebral" (*mūrddhanya*)—this is a governing heading (*adhikāra*). The term "subsequent" applies from this point until the sūtra *ta-āghādanāḍambarāt* (6.3.70), and the term "cerebral" extends up to that limit. *Svar*, *dhūḥ*, and *sāṃsahī* [undergo the cerebral change] before the word *yaḥ*. (6.3.52)

In the words *svaḥ* and *dhūḥ*, as well as in *yathāsaṃkhyam* and *sāmsaha*, the letter *r* becomes a retroflex (*mūrddhanya*) when followed by a retroflex sound; for example, *svarṣām apsām* and *itaṃ dhūrṣāhau*. Regarding the modification: in the case of *yathāsannam*, the letter *ṣ* occurs because of its slight opening (*īṣadvivṛtatvāt*). In the *sthitopasthita* (fixed and adjacent) position, *svaḥ sāmi* becomes *svaḥ sāmi*; *sām dhūḥ sahau* becomes *sāmdhūḥ sahau*. The vowel *u* [is treated] in the *durdde* [section]. 53.

This *visarjanīya* following a short vowel (*durit*) becomes the vowel *u*, and the following [consonant] becomes a retroflex (*mūrddhanya*). Because it is designated as *dhi*, because it is not a sibilant (*asoṣman*), and because it is not nasalized (*niranunāsika*), it becomes the vowel *u*. In the example *pari te dūḍabhaḥ*, according to the rule for *sthitopasthita*, *duḥ* becomes *dūḥ* and *dabhaḥ* becomes *dūḍabhaḥ*. Since it is stated that this occurs in the *upasthita* state, the rule *rephaṃ svaradhāḥ* applies; however, in the *sthita* state, it does not occur because there is no *saṃhitā* (euphonic combination). A *visarjanīya* preceded by the vowel *o* becomes *i* before the root *sic* when it has a penultimate vowel (*sopadha*). (54)

The *visarga* "itaḥ," when followed by the root *siñcati*, becomes the vowel *o* together with its preceding vowel, and the following [consonant] becomes a retroflex (*mūrddhanya*). Example: *parīto ṣiñcatā sutam*. This concludes the rules for the euphonic combination of *visarga*.
Thus ends the *Prātiśākhyapradīpa-śikṣā*.
